en: Uj II.i.1:
To whomever who approaches seeking the going-forth, he should ask about the obstructing factors; having asked, he should cause him to take them up.
Having caused him to take them up, the three goings for refuge and the five precepts—the restraint of a lay follower—should be conferred. And thus:
It should be given again (Upj(J) 16.13–16; cf. Kṣudr-v(Bhī) 9a1–4; Uj II.i.2).

Pay heed, Venerable Sir! I, who am named so-and-so, go for refuge to the Buddha, the foremost of bipeds; I go for refuge to the Dharma, the foremost of those free from passion; I go for refuge to the Saṅgha, the foremost of assemblies.
May the Venerable Sir accept me as a lay follower for as long as life shall last.
In this manner, it should be said a second and a third time as well.
"Pay attention, Preceptor! Just as those noble Arhats, for as long as life lasts, having abandoned the taking of life, [abstained] from the taking of life..."

Having abstained [from these], even so I, named so-and-so, for as long as life lasts, having abandoned the taking of life, abstain from the taking of life. By this first limb, I train after the training of those noble Arhats, I conform to it, and I imitate it.

As those noble Arhats [abstained] for as long as life lasts from taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and the occasion of negligence consisting of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants; (cf. Kṣudr-v(Bhī) 9 b1–4; Uj II.i.3b).

Having abandoned the occasion for negligence consisting of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants, they abstain from them; even so, I, who am named so-and-so, for as long as life lasts, having abandoned taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and the occasion for negligence consisting of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants, abstain from the occasion for negligence consisting of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants.
By this fifth limb, I train after the training and conform to the training of those noble Arhats.
I imitate thus, a second time and a third time.
(Uj II.ii.1.1 See below 1.5.
Uj II.ii.1.2)

Thereafter, a monk who shall announce [the matter] must be requested. The announcing monk must ask: "Have you been instructed in the rules of proper conduct (*āsamudācārika-dharma*)? If he announces [the matter] without having asked this, he becomes guilty of an offense (*sātisāra*).
Uj II.ii.1.3 Afterwards, the monk who makes the announcement must announce it;
furthermore, it should be announced when the entire Saṅgha is seated together in assembly or gathered in a procession.

Having performed the triple salutation (*samīcī-trī*), standing in a squatting posture (*utkuṭuka*) at the end of the assembly, and raising his joined palms (*añjali*), he should speak as follows: "Venerable sirs, please attend to me.
This person, named so-and-so, who is seeking the going-forth (*pravrajyā*), is a householder wearing white garments, with hair and beard not yet shorn."

He desires to go forth in this well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya; this person of such-and-such a name, with such-and-such a name as preceptor, will shave off his hair and beard, don saffron robes, and with perfect faith go forth from the home to the homeless state in this well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya.
"Why should he go forth?
(Upj(J) 8.1–8; ~ Skt.C 44r1–4; cf. Kṣudr-v(Bhī) 10a4–b2) Uj II.ii.1.4.
It should be said by all: "If he is pure, then [say] 'He is pure'. If they say this, it is well; if they do not say this, they commit an offense.

Thereafter, the preceptor (upādhyāya) is to be requested; and he is to be requested in this manner: having arranged his robes properly and standing before him in a squatting position, he should speak as follows:
"Pay attention, O Teacher (ācārya)! I, [name], request the Teacher to be my preceptor. May the Teacher be my preceptor;
with the Teacher as preceptor, I shall go forth. Thus a second and a third time. But at the third utterance, [he says] "Preceptor..."
Thus it should be said (Upj(J) 8.11–15; ~ Skt.C 44r4–5; cf. Kṣudr-v(Bhī) 10b2–4;
Uj II.ii.1.6).
Then he should be ordained; and furthermore, he should be ordained in this manner: "Pay attention, Preceptor!
I, [name], go for refuge to the Buddha, the foremost of bipeds; I go for refuge to the Dharma, the foremost of those free from passion; I go for refuge to the Saṅgha, the foremost of assemblies."

I go forth after that Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Lion of the Śākyas, the Sovereign King of the Śākyas, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha who has gone forth; I cast off the mark of a householder and take up the mark of one who has gone forth. Thus a second and a third time.
Kṣudr-v(Bhī) 11 a5–b4) Uj II.ii.1.7 Thereafter, the hair is to be shorn; they shave off all of it.
The Blessed One said: "The topknot (cūḍā) should be set aside; thereafter, he should be asked: 'Let the topknot be removed.
If he says 'no,' it should be told to him: 'In that case, go right away. But if he says 'let it be removed,' it should be removed."
Thereafter, he should be bathed: if it is the cold season, he should be bathed with warm water; if it is the hot season, with cool water.

Then the preceptor must give him the saffron-colored robes; he, in turn, must receive them by prostrating at the preceptor’s feet. Thereafter, the preceptor must dress him and examine him to ensure that he is not lacking sexual characteristics or possesses both sets of characteristics.

The Blessed One said, "It should be inspected. They, having stripped him naked, inspected him. The Blessed One said, "One should not inspect him by stripping him naked; rather, while he is still clothed, he should be inspected without his being aware of it."
Uj II.ii.2.1 See above 1.6.
Uj II.ii.2.2 Thereafter, a monk should be requested [to perform the ritual].

He who bestows upon him the training precepts for going for refuge should prepare a seat for him, and having sat down before him in a squatting position with palms joined, he should speak as follows: "Pay attention, Venerable Sir! I, named so-and-so, go for refuge to the Buddha, the foremost of bipeds; I go for refuge to the Dharma, the foremost of those free from passion."
I go for refuge to the Saṅgha, the foremost of assemblies.
May the Venerable One accept me as a novice for as long as life shall last.
In this manner, it should be stated a second and a third time during the third recitation: "And may the Preceptor accept me as a novice."
Then he should be made to undertake the training rules.
And furthermore, he should be made to undertake them in this way: "Pay attention, Preceptor! Just as those noble Arhats [abstained] from taking life for as long as they lived..."

Having abandoned the taking of life, they abstain from taking life; even so, I, [name], for as long as life lasts, having abandoned the taking of life, abstain from the taking of life. By this first limb, I train after them, follow, and imitate the training of those noble Arhats.

Just as those noble Arhats, for as long as life lasts, abstained from taking what is not given, unchaste conduct, false speech, the use of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants which are the basis of negligence,
dancing, singing, music, wearing garlands, perfumes, ointments, and cosmetics, using high and large beds, and eating at improper times.

Having abandoned the acceptance of gold and silver, they abstain from accepting gold and silver; in the same way, I, [name], for as long as life lasts, shall abandon taking what is not given, unchaste conduct, false speech, the intoxication of fermented and distilled liquors which is a basis for negligence,
dancing, singing, music, wearing garlands, perfumes, ointments, and cosmetics, using high and large beds, and eating at improper times.
Having abandoned the acceptance of gold and silver, I abstain from the acceptance of gold and silver.
By this tenth limb, I train after the training of those noble Arhats, I conform to it, and I imitate it. Thus, a second and a third time as well.
The formal act of full ordination (upasaṃpadā-karman) is to be performed.

Then, if he has reached the full age of twenty years, his bowl and robes must be sought; a monk who will act as the private instructor (*raho'nuśāsaka*) must be requested; a monk who will perform the ritual act (*karmakāraka*) must be requested; and those monks who will enter the mandala must be requested.

Then, when the entire Saṃgha is seated together or assembled, or in a group of ten within a maṇḍala, one should cause him to perform three prostrations; or two prostrations with the five-pointed salutation (*pañcamaṇḍalaka*), or three prostrations by pressing the shins together (*jāṅghāprapīḍanikā*). Having caused him to perform these three prostrations, he should request the preceptor (*upādhyāya*); if it is the preceptor himself, or otherwise the teacher (*ācārya*).

The preceptor is the venerable one; and furthermore, he is to be requested as follows: having performed the proper salutation toward the preceptor, sitting before him with his heels [together] on bricks, and raising his joined palms, this should be said: (Upj(J) 11.5–10;
Uj II.iii.1.1.2.2)
Pay attention, Preceptor! I, named so-and-so, request the Preceptor as my preceptor. May the Preceptor be my preceptor;
through the Preceptor as preceptor, I shall receive full ordination. Thus a second and a third time.
But regarding the Teacher (ācārya), on the third utterance, one should say "Venerable Sir" (*bhadanta*) instead of "Preceptor" (*upādhyāya*).
Then, the robes should be formally determined (*adhiṣṭhāpayitavya*). If they are already cut, they should be determined in this way:
"Pay attention, Preceptor! I, named so-and-so, determine this robe as an outer cloak (*sāṃghāṭī*), which has been finished and completed."
"A robe that is permissible and fit for use"—thus a second and a third time.
(Upj(J) 11.13–15; ~ Skt.C 45 r5–6; cf. Kṣudr-v(Bhī) 15 a1–2;
Uj II.iii.1.1.3.1b)
Pay attention, Preceptor: I, [name], designate this robe as an upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*). It is a robe that is finished, proper, and fit for use.
This should be said a second and a third time.
"Pay attention, Preceptor! I, [name], designate this robe as an inner garment (*antarvāsa*); it is a finished robe, suitable, and fit for use. This should be said a second and a third time. (Upj(J))
11.18–20; ~ Skt.C 45 r7–v1; cf. Kṣudr-v(Bhī) 15 a2) Uj II.iii.1.1.3.2a:
If [the robes] have not been cut, they must be consecrated in this way: "Pay attention, Preceptor! I, named so-and-so..."

I consecrate this robe, the outer cloak (saṃghāṭī). Desiring to make it new, with two and a half circular patches, I shall wash it without hindrance, stretch it, cut it, sew it together, join it, finish it, dye it, or attach patches to it;
or I shall prepare it according to the available materials. This robe is permissible.
The same should be said for the *pāribhogika* [robe] a second and a third time. (Upj(J) 12.1–5;
~ Skt.C 45v1–3) "Pay attention, Preceptor! I, named so-and-so, consecrate this robe as an upper garment (*uttarāsaṅga*)."

Desiring [to complete] the sevenfold process, I shall make two and a half circles; I shall run without hindrance; I shall spread it out, cut it, join it, knot it, sew it, dye it, or attach patches, and I shall act according to the requirements so that this robe-cloth becomes fit and suitable for use. Thus a second time, and thus a third time.
Furthermore, it should be said:

"Pay attention, Preceptor! I, [name], am designating this robe-material as an inner garment (*antarvāsa*). Desiring to make it five spans, I shall make it one and a half *maṇḍalaka* patches; I will wear it without any hindrance."

"I will spread it out, I will cut it, I will join it together, I will sew it, I will treat it, I will preserve it, or I will have attendants apply it; I will act according to the requirements. This robe-cloth is suitable and fit for use."
In this manner, it should be said a second and a third time.
Then, the bowl should be shown to the Saṃgha [with the words]: "This is his bowl; may it not be a deficient bowl or an excessive bowl."
Uj II.iii.1.1.5:
Then it must be authorized, and furthermore, it must be authorized in this manner:
Having placed the bowl in the left hand and covered it with the right hand, one should say: "Pay attention, Preceptor!
I, [name], consecrate this bowl—the vessel of the sages, the vessel for alms—as a utensil for use in eating. This should be said a second and a third time in the same manner.

Thereafter, having moved away from the vicinity of the ascetics (śramaṇopavicāra) and into the vicinity of the [monastic] assembly (darśanopavicāra), he should be made to stand facing the community with his hands joined in reverence (añjali).
Then, the officiating monk (karmakāraka) should ask: "Who has been requested by [the candidate] named so-and-so on behalf of [the preceptor] named so-and-so?"
Regarding the "private instructor" (*raho'nuśāsaka*): he who has been appointed must say, "I am [so-and-so] by name.
(Upj(J) 13.1-4; ~ Skt.C 46 r2; cf. Kṣudr-v(Bhī) 15 a5-b1;
Uj II.iii.1.2.2)
Thereafter, he should be encouraged. He should be asked:
"Are you able to instruct [the candidate] in secret, [acting as] preceptor for one named so-and-so? By him it should be said: "I am able."
Then, the monk acting as the officiant (karmakāraka) should perform the formal motion (jñapti):
"May the venerable Saṅgha listen. This monk, named so-and-so, is capable of instructing in private the monk named so-and-so."

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, let the Saṃgha authorize that the monk named so-and-so, with the preceptor named so-and-so, be appointed as the private instructor for the monk named so-and-so; this monk named so-and-so shall instruct the monk named so-and-so in private with the preceptor named so-and-so. This is the motion.
Thereafter, the monk acting as the private instructor, having caused [the candidate] to perform the proper ritual acts toward himself, should have him sit in the *utkuṭuka* posture.
Having raised his joined palms, this should be said: "Listen, venerable one; this is the time for truth, this is the time for reality.
Whatever I ask you, you must answer with confidence: what is real, as real;
and what is unreal, as unreal, and explain it accordingly."
13.13–17; ~ Skt.C 46r5–7; cf. Kṣudr-v(Bhī) 16a1–2) Uj II.iii.1.3.2:
"You are a man, you are a male, you are endowed with the male faculty, you are fully twenty years of age, you are fully twenty years of age, and your three robes and bowl are complete."
[The procedure is] complete.

If his parents are living and he says they are, it should be said: "Have you been authorized by your mother and father? If he says they are deceased, it should be said: "Are you not a slave, nor one who has reached [the age of] servitude, nor one who is subject to verbal command?"

Do not be one who has been brought away by force, nor one who has been sold, nor a royal soldier, nor a criminal against the king, nor one who performs acts detrimental to the king; have you not yourself committed or caused to be committed an act detrimental to the king?
Are you not a thief with a banner displayed, nor a eunuch, nor a paṇḍaka, nor one lacking sexual organs, nor one possessing both sets of sexual organs?

Do not be one who violates a nun; do not be a matricide, a patricide, a murderer of an Arhat, a schismatic of the Saṅgha, or one who with malicious intent draws blood from a Tathāgata; do not be a heretic, nor one who has entered into heresy;
do not be one who lives in common through theft, nor one who lives apart, nor one who is not in communion; do not be a phantom; and let there be nothing whatsoever belonging to anyone for you.
If he says, "Whether it be little or much, it must be given," one should say, "Will you be able to give after you have gone forth?
If he says "No," one should say, "Then go right back. If he says, "I will be able," one should say, "It must be given."
"Three months ago you previously went forth.
If he says, "I have gone forth," it should be said: "Among the four *pārājika* offenses, have you committed any one of them?"
If one who has committed an offense, through confusion, says, "I have properly laid aside the training," he should be told, "In that very case, go.
If he says, "No," he should be asked, "Have you now gone forth?
If he says, "I have gone forth," he should be told, "You have practiced the holy life correctly."
"Have you practiced [the precepts]? What is your name? What is the name of your preceptor? "For the sake of the matter, I shall state my name: my preceptor’s name is so-and-so."
Listen, venerable one; indeed, such bodily afflictions as these occur in men, namely:

leprosy, boils, scabs, ringworm, eczema, itch, scabies, herpes, psoriasis, hiccups, vomiting, cholera, hemorrhoids, blood disorders, bile disorders, abdominal tumors, fistula-in-ano, consumption, cough, asthma, wasting, and epilepsy.
May such bodily afflictions as hemorrhoids, jaundice, aching limbs, aching bones, aching sides, urinary diseases, dysentery, elephantiasis,
exhaustion, fever, high fever, quotidian fever, tertian fever, quartan fever, fever arising from the derangement of all three humors (*sāṃnipātika*),
continuous fever, or irregular fever— not these nor any others of a similar kind— be found in your body. (Upj(J))
"That which has just now been asked of you by me, that very same thing your fellow-practitioners will ask you in the midst of the Saṃgha; there too..."
Being confident, one should speak what is true as true and confess what is untrue as untrue, saying:
"Stay! Do not come until you have been summoned."

Thereafter, the monk acting as the private instructor, standing on the path inside, should say: "Listen, venerable Saṅgha; I, named so-and-so, have been instructed in secret by the preceptor named so-and-so regarding the obstructing factors."
What should come?
(Upj(J) 16.10–12; ~ Skt.C 47r6–7; cf. Kṣudr-v(Bhī) 17a4–5) Uj II.iii.2.1.2.
It should be said by all: "If he is pure.
If they say so, it is well; if they do not say so, they become guilty of an offense.

Thereafter, having caused the monk who is the candidate for ordination to perform the proper ritual acts, he should be made to sit on his haunches before the bricks and, having raised his joined palms, be made to request ordination; and furthermore, he should be made to request it in this manner:
(Upj(J))
17.7–9; cf. Kṣudr-v(Bhī) 17a5–b1; 18b5–19a2; KaVā(Bhī) V1) Uj II.iii.2.1.3b:
“Let the venerable Saṃgha listen. I, [name], for the sake of a purpose—here I take my name—[I am] under the preceptor named [name].”

Seeking full ordination, I, who am named so-and-so, request full ordination from the Saṅgha. For the sake of clarity, I state my name: may the venerable Saṅgha ordain me with [the preceptor] named so-and-so as my preceptor;
may the venerable Saṅgha lift me up; may the venerable Saṅgha favor me; may the venerable Saṅgha have compassion for me; may the venerable Saṅgha, being compassionate, [grant me ordination].
Out of compassion, [he said] thus a second and a third time.
Thereafter, the monk acting as the ritual officiant (*karmakāraka*) must perform the *muktikā-jñapti* (the formal motion consisting of a single statement).

"May the venerable Saṃgha listen. This person, named so-and-so, seeking full ordination from the one named so-and-so, requests full ordination from the Saṃgha with so-and-so as preceptor. If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and if the Saṃgha permits, may the Saṃgha authorize us to question this person, named so-and-so, regarding the obstructing factors within the midst of the Saṃgha."
With such-and-such a name as preceptor, this is the motion (*jñapti*).
(Upj(J) 17.15–18.2; ~ Skt.C 47 v2–4; cf. Kṣudr-v(Bhī) 17 b3–5; 19 a4–b1; KaVā(Bhī) V3–4;
Uj II.iii.2.2.2)
Thereafter, it should be said: "Listen, venerable one! This is your time for truth, this is your time for reality," and so on as before, up to: "or others of a similar kind."

Thereafter, having made the motion (*jñapti*), the formal act (*karman*) should be performed; and it should be performed in this way: "Let the venerable Saṅgha listen. This man, named so-and-so, seeks full ordination from the one named so-and-so; he is twenty years of age, and his three robes and bowl are complete."
He declares himself pure regarding the obstructing factors. This person, of such-and-such a name, requests full ordination from the Saṃgha with such-and-such a name as preceptor.

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and if the Saṃgha consents, let the Saṃgha authorize that the Saṃgha ordain this person of such-and-such a name with such-and-such a name as preceptor. This is the motion (*jñapti*).

Thus the ritual action should be performed: "Listen, venerable Saṅgha! This person named so-and-so, seeking full ordination from the one named so-and-so, is twenty years of age, and his three robes and bowl are complete."
He declares himself pure with respect to the obstructing factors.

This person, named so-and-so, requests full ordination from the Saṅgha with the preceptor named so-and-so. Therefore, the Saṅgha grants full ordination to this person named so-and-so with the preceptor named so-and-so. To those venerable ones for whom it is agreeable to grant full ordination to this person named so-and-so...
With such-and-such a name as preceptor, those who consent [to this] remain silent; those who do not consent should speak. This is the first formal proclamation (*karmavācanā*);
in the same way, the second and third formal proclamations are to be recited.

This person, named so-and-so, has been ordained by the Saṃgha with such-and-such a person as preceptor. It is approved and permitted by the Saṃgha, because it is silent; thus do I understand this to be so.
Thereafter, the shadow must be measured.
It was said by the Blessed One: "The shadow must be measured."
The monks measured with their footsteps, and it took too long. The Blessed One said:
"It should not be measured by footsteps; it should be measured with a measuring-stick. The monks measured with one that was too long.
Nevertheless, it takes too long.
The Blessed One said:
"It should be measured with a peg four finger-breadths in length; as many pegs as there are, so many men should be stated [to have passed]."
18.21–19.2; cf. Kṣudr-v(Bhī) 21b5–22a2) Uj II.iii.3.2:
Thereafter, the time must be announced—whether it be the forenoon, midday, afternoon, or the first watch of the night.
The first watch, the middle half-watch, the last watch; the first watch, the middle half-watch, the last watch; when the dawn has not yet arisen, when the dawn has arisen;
when the sun has not yet risen, when the sun has risen; when the sun has risen one-eighth of its course, when the sun has risen one-fourth of its course;
when midday has not yet passed, when midday has passed; when one-fourth of the day remains, when one-eighth of the day remains.
The sun has not set; the sun has set.
The stars have not risen; the stars have risen.
Thereafter, the seasonal periods must be announced: there are five seasonal periods— the winter, the summer, the rainy season, the late rainy season, and [the period] following the rainy season.
The long rainy season consists of four winter months—Mārgaśīrṣa, Pauṣa, Māgha, and Phālguna;
four summer months—Caitra, Vaiśākha, Jyeṣṭha, and Āṣāḍha; one month of the rainy season—Śrāvaṇa;
and one day and night of the "end-of-rainy" period—the first day of the month of Bhādrapada. The long rainy season thus comprises three months minus one night.
Bhādrapada, Āśvayuja, and Kārttika.
Kṣudr-v(Bhī) 22 a2-4) Uj III.i.1 Thereafter, the four reliances (*niśraya*) should be announced: "Listen, venerable one, these four [reliances] were [established] by that Blessed One..."

The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened one, who knows and sees, has thus declared the supports for a monk who has gone forth and received full ordination—those supports by relying upon which a monk’s going forth, full ordination, and status as a monk exist within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya.
What are these four? (Upj(J))
19.15–19; ~ Skt.C 48r6–7; cf. Kṣudr-v(Bhī) 22a5–b2) Uj III.i.2.1:
Among robes, the rag-robe (*pāṃsukūla*) is both permissible and easy to obtain, and it is by relying upon this that a monk [thrives] in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya.

"Going forth, full ordination, and the state of a monk: O [Name], are you able to subsist for as long as life lasts on robes made of discarded rags? He should reply, "I am able. "As for additional gains: silk cloths, woven cotton cloths, or woolen blankets."
Whether they be made of fine cotton, of silk, or of linen.
Or linen,
or cotton,
or hemp.
Whether it be made of cotton, or of *āmilā* fibers, or of *somilā* fibers, or of *kṛmilā* fibers, or the color of *kṛmi* insects.
Or of uniform color; or of beautiful color; or of ugly color.
Whether it be fine cloth from Kāśī,

fine linen, fine *dukūla* silk, or fine *koṭṭambaka* cotton— whatever other suitable robe-material (*cīvara*) may arise, whether from the Saṅgha or from an individual— in that case as well, you must exercise moderation in accepting it.
"Will you fully awaken to such a state?
He should say, "I shall fully awaken."
Listen, [you] of such-and-such a name: alms-food is among foods both permissible and easily obtained.

Relying upon which, for a monk in this well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, there is the going forth, the full ordination, and the state of a monk. Are you, [you] of such-and-such a name, able to subsist for as long as life lasts on alms-food as your nourishment?
He should say: "I am able [to accept] extra gains, whether they be meals, or refreshments, or drinks of gruel;
whether they be regular offerings, or invitations, or those occurring on the fifth day."
Or on the eighth day,
or on the fourteenth day,
or on the fifteenth day.
Or an alms-offering arising from a portent;
or a lumped-together gift;
or whatever other suitable alms-food may arise, whether from the Saṅgha or from an individual.
In that regard as well, you must exercise moderation in accepting gifts, thinking: "Will I be able to fully awaken to such a state?
He should say: "I shall fully awaken."
Listen, [you] of such-and-such a name!
Among the lodgings, the root of a tree is suitable and easily obtained; relying upon this, a monk [should dwell] in the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya.
"Going forth and full ordination constitute the state of a monk. O [Name], are you able to spend your life with a tree root as your lodging?
He should say: 'I am able.
As for additional gains: either dwellings or garlands."
Or gabled halls, or turrets, or watchtowers, or palaces.
Or a hut made of hair-tips, or one with a back like an *āmalaka* fruit,
or a cave in the earth.
Whether it be a mountain cave, a cliffside cave,
or a shelter made of grass mats.
Or leaf-huts, or grass huts, or leaf-shelters.
Whether they have practiced walking meditation or not,
or whether they have practiced the practice of inclining the body forward;
"Or, 'not having made a prior commitment'—that is, whatever other suitable bedding and seating may arise from the Saṅgha or from an individual, you must exercise moderation in accepting even that.
"Will you be able to master such a state?
He should say, "I shall master it."

Listen, [you] of such-and-such a name: there is this purgative medicine, which is suitable, easily obtained, and by relying upon which, for a monk in this well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, there is going forth, full ordination, and the status of a monk. Are you, [you] of such-and-such a name, able to [use it] for as long as life lasts?

"To subsist on medicine that has become putrid, he should say: 'I am able. Extra acquisitions include ghee, oil, honey, molasses, [medicines] for a day, for a watch of the night, for seven days, or for as long as life lasts."
Root medicine, stem medicine, leaf medicine, flower medicine, fruit medicine,
or whatever other suitable medicine may arise from the Saṅgha or from an individual— in that regard as well, you must exercise moderation in accepting it.
"Will you fully awaken to such a state?
He should reply, "I shall fully awaken."
Thereafter, the four *patanīya* dharmas (offenses involving defeat) must be proclaimed.
Furthermore, they should be proclaimed in this manner: "Listen, you of such-and-such a name; these four [dharmas] were [proclaimed] by that Blessed One who knows..."

The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened one, having seen [this], has thus declared the *patanīya* dharmas for a monk who has gone forth and received full ordination; by committing any one of these points, a monk becomes, upon that very transgression, no longer a monk, no longer a *śramaṇa*, no longer a son of the Śākyas; he falls from the state of a monk, and his status as a *śramaṇa* is destroyed.
His asceticism is ruined, crushed, fallen, defeated, and beyond recovery.
(Upj(J) 21.16–21; ~ Skt.C 49v5–50r1; cf. Kṣudr-v(Bhī) 23b2–5;
Uj III.ii.1.2)
Just as a palmyra tree cut off at the crown is incapable of becoming green again, and incapable of growth, increase, or expansion,

even so a monk who commits any one of these four points becomes, with that very commission, no longer a monk, no longer a śramaṇa, no longer a son of the Śākyas; he falls from the state of a monk, and his [monkhood] is destroyed.
His state of a śramaṇa is destroyed, crushed, fallen, and defeated; his state of a śramaṇa becomes irrecoverable.
Which four? (Upj(J) 22.1; cf. Kṣudr-v(Bhī) 23 b5–24 a2)

Venerable sir, in many ways the Blessed One has censured sensual pleasures; he has praised the abandoning of sensual pleasures, their relinquishment, their casting off, their disappearance, their destruction, their fading away, their cessation, their stilling, and their subsiding— namely, the dwelling in sensual pleasures, the bondage of sensual pleasures, the obsession with sensual pleasures, and the determination for sensual pleasures.
"O Venerable One, you have been exhorted, praised, lauded, extolled, and commended: from this day forward, with a mind free from passion,
you must not look upon a woman with a lustful eye, let alone engage in unchaste sexual intercourse through the union of the two organs."

Kṣudr-v(Bhī) 24a2–5) And this has been said, O Venerable One, by that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly awakened Buddha, who knows and sees: Uj III.ii.2.1.2.1.2. [The text continues with the specific rule.]

Furthermore, if a monk who has entered into the proper observance of the training together with other monks, without having renounced the training and without having disclosed his weakness in the training, should practice unchaste sexual intercourse— even down to [intercourse] with an animal— [this constitutes a pārājika offense].
A monk who commits such an offense becomes, by that very commission, no longer a monk, no longer a śramaṇa, no longer a son of the Śākyas;
he falls from the state of a monk. His status as a śramaṇa is destroyed, ruined, shattered, fallen, defeated, and lost.
His state of being a śramaṇa becomes irrevocable.
Just as a palm tree, once severed at the crown, is incapable of remaining green, and incapable of attaining growth, increase, or expansion.
(Upj(J) 22.11–12; ~ Skt.C 50v1; cf. Kṣudr-v(Bhī) 24b3;
Uj III.ii.2.1.4)
In the same way, monks, when a monk has committed such an offense,
his status as a śramaṇa is lost immediately upon that commission, to the point that it cannot be restored. Therefore, from this day forward,
you must apply yourselves with intense mental protection, mindfulness, and vigilance to not transgress, to not commit [such an act], and to abstaining from transgression.
22.12–15; ~ Skt.C 50 v1–2; cf. Kṣudr-v(Bhī) 24 b3–5) Upj III.ii.2.1.5:
“Will you not commit such an offense? He should say: “I will not commit it. (Upj(J))
Kṣudr-v(Bhī) 24 b5) Uj III.ii.2.2.1 Listen, venerable one: in many ways the Blessed One has censured taking what is not given and praised the abstention from taking what is not given.

"O Venerable One, you have been praised, extolled, described, and lauded. From this day forward, you must not, with a mind intent on theft, take what belongs to another even so much as the husk of a sesame seed without it being given; what need is there to mention five months' worth or more than five months' worth?"
And this was said, O Venerable One, by that Blessed One— the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One— who knows and sees:
"If a monk should take from others what has not been given, whether in a village or in the forest, and which is reckoned as theft..."

If, by means of such taking what has not been given, a king or a royal official should seize him and either kill him, bind him, or banish him, and say to him: "Fie upon you, man! You are a thief, you are a fool, you are deluded, you are a robber! (Upj(J) 23.1-5; ~ Skt.C 50 v5-7; cf. Kṣudr-v(Bhī) 25 a2-4)
In this way,

by committing such an act, a monk ceases to be a monk by the very fact of that commission— just as a palm tree cut off at its crown cannot grow again— as long as he does not resolve: "I shall never commit it again."

"Listen, venerable one! In many ways the Blessed One has censured the taking of life; he has praised, extolled, lauded, and commended the abstention from taking life. From this day forward, venerable one, you must not intentionally take life, even so much as an ant."
Not even a single living being is to be deprived of life, let alone a human or one who has the form of a human.
(Upj(J) 23.7–10; ~ Skt.C 51 r1–3; cf. Kṣudr-v(Bhī) 25 a5–b1;
Uj III.ii.2.3.2)
And this has been said, O Venerable One, by that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, who knows and sees:

"If a monk should intentionally, with his own hand, deprive a human being or one having human form of life; or should provide him with a weapon, or seek out a weapon-bearer for him, or should incite him toward death..."
Or he might describe the dispraise of death to him and say to him: "O man, what use have you for this evil, impure, and wretched life?
O man, death is better for you than life. With thoughts approved by his own mind and with mental intentions, he might in many ways urge him toward death or describe the dispraise of death to him.
And he might die by that means (Upj(J) 23.10-16;
~ Skt.C 51 r3-v1; cf. Kṣudr-v(Bhī) 25 b1-4) Uj III.ii.2.3.3.

Having committed such an offense, a monk, by the very fact of that commission, ceases to be a monk, ceases to be a śramaṇa, ceases to be a son of the Śākyas— as previously stated— until [he says], "I shall not commit it again."

Listen, venerable one, in many ways the Blessed One has censured false speech; he has praised, extolled, lauded, and commended the abstention from false speech. From this day forward, venerable one, you must not speak a deliberate falsehood, even as a joke, let alone to boast of a superhuman state that is non-existent and unreal. (Upj(J))
Kṣudr-v(Bhī) 26 a1–2) Uj III.ii.2.4.2.1 And this has been said, O Venerable One, by that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, who knows and sees:

Furthermore, if a monk, not knowing and not fully understanding, should claim—while lacking and not possessing it—that he has attained a superhuman state, a distinction of noble realization, or knowledge, vision, or a state of abiding in contact, saying, "I know this;
I see this," [and being asked] "What do you know? [he replies] "I know suffering; I know its origin, its cessation, and the path"; what [does he know]?

I see the gods, I see the nāgas, yakṣas, garuḍas, gandharvas, kinnaras, mahoragas, pretas, piśācas, kumbhāṇḍas, and kaṭapūtanas; the gods also see me, and the nāgas, yakṣas, garuḍas, gandharvas, kinnaras, mahoragas,
pretas, piśācas, kumbhāṇḍas, and kaṭapūtanas also see me.

“I hear the voices of the gods, and I hear the voices of the nāgas, up to and including the kaṭapūtanas; the gods also hear my voice, and the nāgas, up to and including the kaṭapūtanas, also hear my voice.”
I approach to see the gods;
I approach to see the nāgas, up to and including the kaṭapūtanas.
The gods also approach to see me; the nāgas, up to and including the kaṭapūtanas, also approach to see me.

I converse with the gods, I talk with them, I greet them, and I even engage in continuous discourse with them; likewise, I converse, talk, greet, and even engage in continuous discourse with the *nāgas*, up to and including the *kaṭapūtanas*. The gods also converse with me, talk with me, greet me, and even engage in continuous discourse with me; so too do the *nāgas*, up to and including...
Even the *kaṭapūtana* spirits converse with me, talk with me, exchange greetings, and even enter into continuous discourse with me.
While not having actually attained the perception of impermanence, one claims of oneself, "I am an attainer of it. Likewise, while not having attained the perception of suffering in the impermanent,

the perception of non-self in what is suffering, the perception of repulsiveness in food, the perception of disenchantment with the entire world, the perception of danger, the perception of abandonment, the perception of dispassion, the perception of cessation, or the perception of death— (Upj(J))
24.15–18; ~ Skt.C 52 r6–v2; cf. Kṣudr-v(Bhī) 26 b5–27 a2; ŚrBh(T:

re-ed) I 214.2–5) Uj III.ii.2.4.2.3b Even while not having attained the perception of the foul (*aśubhasaṃjñā*), one claims of oneself, "I am one who has attained it," regarding the perception of the livid corpse (*vinīlakasaṃjñā*).

He claims of himself: "I am one who has attained the perception of the festering, the perception of the bloated, the perception of the dismembered, the perception of the devoured, the perception of the bloody, the perception of the scattered, the perception of the bones, and the perception of the contemplation of emptiness. (Upj(J))
24.18–20; ~ Skt.C 52 v2–4; cf. Kṣudr-v(Bhī) 27 a2–3; ŚrBh(T: re-ed) I 214.5–8) Uj III.ii.2.4.2.4.
While still not having attained the first dhyāna, the second, the third, or the fourth dhyāna...

of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; of the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; of the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning; of the domain of supernatural power, the divine ear, knowledge of the minds of others, recollection of former abodes, knowledge of death and rebirth, and the destruction of the outflows. (Upj(J))
24.20–25; ~ Skt.C 52v4–53r1; cf. Kṣudr-v(Bhī) 27a3–b1; ŚrBh(T: re-ed) I 214.8–12) Upj III.ii.2.4.2.5:
Even though he is not an Arhat, one who is not an Arhat claims of himself, "I am an Arhat, a meditator on the eight liberations," except in the case of overweening pride (abhimāna). (Upj(J))
24.25–25.1; ~ Skt.C 53 r1; cf. Kṣudr-v(Bhī) 27 b1) Uj III.ii.2.4.3.1:
Having committed such an offense, by the very fact of its commission, a monk ceases to be a monk, ceases to be a śramaṇa, and ceases to be a son of the Śākyas.
He is deprived of the state of a monk; his status as a śramaṇa is destroyed, ruined, shattered, fallen, defeated,
and his status as a śramaṇa becomes irredeemable.
Just as a palmyra tree cut off at the crown is incapable of becoming green again, incapable of attaining growth, increase, or expansion.

In this very same way, a monk who has committed such an offense— one for which his status as a śramaṇa cannot be restored— must, from this day forward, apply himself with intense effort toward non-transgression, non-offense, and the abstention from transgression.
One should apply oneself to the guarding of the mind through mindfulness and heedfulness.
"Will you not fall into such a situation? He should say, "I will not fall into it.
(Upj(J) 25.7–8; ~ Skt.C 53 r5; cf. Kṣudr-v(Bhī) 27 b5;
Uj III.iii.1)
Thereafter, the four factors that constitute the state of a śramaṇa must be announced; furthermore, they should be announced in this way:

"Listen, venerable one! These four factors that constitute the state of a śramaṇa were proclaimed by that Blessed One—the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One—who knows and sees—for a monk who has thus gone forth and received full ordination. What are the four? (Upj(J))
25.10–13; ~ Skt.C 53r5–7; cf. Kṣudr-v(Bhī) 31a3–4) Uj III.iii.2:
"From this day forward, venerable one, when you are reviled, you must not revile in return; when you are provoked to anger, you must not provoke anger in return."
"When struck, one should not strike back; when reviled, one should not revile in return. Will you not fall into such a situation?
He should say, "I will not fall into it."

"Listen, venerable one: he who formerly was your aspirant, thinking, 'May I obtain the going forth, the full ordination, and the state of a monk within the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya'— that very person has now gone forth and been fully ordained with a suitable preceptor."

[He is] ordained by two suitable preceptors, by the complete Saṃgha, through a formal act consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapticaturtha-karman*), which is unshakeable and not subject to suspension.
(Upj(J) 25.17–20; ~ Skt.C 53v1–4; cf. Kṣudr-v(Bhī) 31a5–b1;
Upj III.iv.2)
In that which a monk ordained for a hundred years must train in, there he who is ordained this very day must train;

and in that which he who is ordained this very day must train in, there he who is ordained for a hundred years must train. Therefore, from this day forward, you must fulfill—and never fail—that state of having identical morality, identical training, and identical recitation of the Prātimokṣa Sūtra.
25.20–26.1; ~ Skt.C 53 v4–6; cf. Kṣudr-v(Bhī) 31 b1–3) Uj III.iv.3:
From this day forward, you should maintain the perception of your preceptor as a father, and your preceptor should likewise maintain the perception of you as a son.
From this day forward, you must attend upon your preceptor for as long as life lasts; your preceptor, in turn, must attend upon you when you are ill until death or until recovery.

From this day forward, you must dwell with reverence, with deference, and with a sense of awe and submissiveness toward your fellow practitioners of the holy life—whether they be seniors, those of middle standing, or juniors.
(Upj(J) 26.4–6; ~ Skt.C 54 r1–2; cf. Kṣudr-v(Bhī) 31 b5–32 a1) Uj III.iv.5

From this day forward, you must teach, recite, and study; you must cultivate skill in the aggregates (*skandha*), skill in the elements (*dhātu*), skill in the sense-bases (*āyatana*), skill in dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and skill in what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna*).

Furthermore, you must not cast off the burden for the sake of attaining what has not been attained, for the sake of realizing what has not been realized, and for the sake of manifesting what has not been manifested.

These most fundamental training rules have been declared to you by me; you will hear others when the Prātimokṣa Sūtra is recited every half-month, and others still your preceptors and teachers, as well as those with the same preceptor, those with the same teacher, and those who are conversant, familiar, intimate, and affectionate, will cause you to grasp.
Now that you have received full ordination in the teaching of the One of Excellent Wisdom, do not let this rare perfection of the opportune moment go to waste.

The going forth of one who is pleasing and the full ordination of one who is pure have been proclaimed by the Truly Named One, the Fully Awakened One, who possesses knowledge: "Venerable one, you are fully ordained; accomplish this with heedfulness."
The formal motion for full ordination is concluded. // // //
